market.title: AI stocks bounce back — with one notable exception
market.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios The AI trade has regained momentum despite — or maybe because of — Nvidia's struggles following the weekend revelations from CEO Jensen Huang. The big picture: Monday's sudden burst of exuberance for AI was the latest wide swing for a market upended by last week's "blue tsunami" in the midterm elections and the threat they could pose to the data center boom. By the numbers: The Nasdaq 100 index of large-cap technology shares soared 3.4%, its biggest daily jump since late March and its second-best showing of the year. Zoom in: Stocks romped across the AI ecosystem — well, with one important exception. Pick-and-shovel plays such as engineering and construction companies, and makers of data center inputs like fiberoptic cables, servers and data storage devices soared. The companies that build and lease out data center computing power, known as neoclouds, also jumped. (Those companies had been at the epicenter of recent jitters about financing for the AI boom.) Hyperscalers rose, paced by Meta, which notched a gain of 5.1%. Semiconductors roared, with the SOX index posting its best gain — 6.9% — since late July. Yes, but: The glaring exception to the AI-palooza was its best-known player, Nvidia. Weekend revelations from CEO Jensen Huang — who acknowledged having an affair with a woman suspected of connections to Chinese intelligence — left investors grappling with uncertainty about the CEO's future. The intrigue: Some investors may see Nvidia's pain as potential gain for rivals. Broadcom jumped 8.8%, its best day in nearly a year. Advanced Micro Devices soared 13.3%, benefiting also from an upgrade to "Outperform" — effectively, a "buy" recommendation — from Oppenheimer analysts on Sunday. Context: Bullish commentary from Wall Street established the background music for Monday's big bounce, as analysts urged investors to buy into the market's recent soft patch. "We believe stocks are now clearly in oversold territory," Goldman Sachs analysts wrote in a note Monday. "We believe the market's reaction to the midterms is overdone," wrote Morgan Stanley tech analysts in a note entitled "Buy the Drop: AI Investment Opportunities Post the U.S. Midterms," which it published Sunday night. "We do not think AI is a continued sell here. In fact, tech drawdown is offering certain opportunities. The selloff was very sharp," JPMorgan equity strategists wrote Monday. These analysts could be right. The recent slump has been deep in certain sectors such as chips. And buying the dip has been a solid strategy in recent years, especially for retail investors . The other side: On the other hand, there may be good reasons such stocks sold off. For example, even before the news about the Nvidia CEO or the anti-data center vote at the polls, Wall Street expectations for capital expenditures from hyperscalers had been looking a bit flat. Given that a large percentage of that AI investment is spent on the semiconductors needed to make these computing centers, well, compute, that would seem to be important for tech investors. What's next: Will the stock market's rally be the start of a new phase of AI exuberance? Or is it just an example of Wall Street's proverbial dead cat bounce ?

market.title: How Nvidia crisis, politics could deliver the pause AI leaders want
market.summary: A political backlash against AI and data centers — now compounded by a crisis facing the technology's most influential champion — could help force a slowdown that industry leaders have struggled to achieve voluntarily. Why it matters: Tapping the brakes on AI development — which frontier AI developers claim to want but have so far failed to do given the risk of offering an advantage to a competitor — could give society more time to prepare for economic upheaval and the risks of superintelligent systems. A wave of Democratic victories and data center moratoriums are now joined by a potentially weakened Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who admitted to having a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang, who has led the industry in barreling through past resistance to AI acceleration, may be less able to do so while under a microscope. While both factors could stymie data center expansion in the U.S., it's far from clear that would slow AI's advance. Between the lines: Huang has been a powerful counterweight to calls for AI restraint, dismissing fears of an AI bubble or purported catastrophic risks to humanity from the technology. An investigation — by the board, an ascendant Democratic congress or federal authorities — could curb his ability to make the case for continued expansion, leaving an opening for those calling for more restrictions. Nvidia says Huang will remain CEO and the news won't slow the company, but the potential impact on his political influence is hard to measure. The potential impact extends beyond that as well. Nvidia is both the dominant supplier of AI chips and an investor in companies building AI infrastructure. A crisis that raises questions about its leadership, business practices or financial relationships could ripple through the industry's expansion plans. The intrigue: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk have all warned about the potentially catastrophic risks of advanced AI, with all expressing, at times, the need to slow or pace the development of advanced AI. But the competitive race has made it difficult for any one company to hit the brakes without risking falling behind rivals or China in a high-stakes race for supremacy. What they're saying: Anthony Aguirre, CEO of the Future of Life Institute, says a slowdown in data center construction would be welcome, even if it wouldn't accomplish nearly as much as more direct restrictions on frontier AI development. "I'll take whatever I can get," Aguirre told Axios in an interview. Aguirre and a number of other researchers have long seen the development of increasingly powerful AI as an existential threat. But he is skeptical that slowing data center construction alone would buy society an additional year or two, given the vast computing resources companies already possess and the growing ability of AI systems to help improve themselves. Aguirre said the bigger opportunity may be political: Resistance to data centers could help generate momentum for legislation and regulation that more directly limits the development of potentially dangerous AI systems. The big picture: Aguirre argues that the goal shouldn't simply be to delay superintelligence by a year or two, but to reconsider whether humanity should build it at all. He favors a "pause and pivot" toward AI systems designed to augment human abilities rather than replace them. Other researchers and executives favor continued development with stronger safeguards, reflecting a broader debate over how much restraint is necessary and what form it should take. Yes, but: Slowing data center construction in the U.S. doesn't necessarily mean slowing AI progress globally. Meta and other companies are exploring data center construction outside the U.S. Google announced a plan this week to invest $15 billion over two years in Malaysia. And Chinese AI developers wouldn't face the same U.S. restrictions, potentially allowing them to narrow the gap with American competitors. The other side: The threat from China isn't as straightforward as it appears. Chinese AI companies benefit in part from distillation of leading American models and technical knowledge developed in the U.S., Aguirre said. Slowing the American frontier could therefore have some effect on China's pace as well. A U.S. decision to slow frontier development could open the door to direct conversations with China about mutually pacing the technology, rather than treating superintelligence as an unavoidable arms race. The bottom line: The AI industry is hoping to overcome political resistance and keep building. Advocates of slowing frontier AI see an opportunity to turn that resistance into something bigger: A chance to reconsider not just how fast AI should advance, but how far it should go.

VALN.title: Valneva annonce un taux de séroréponse de 94% cinq ans après une dose unique du vaccin contre le chikungunya IXCHIQ®
VALN.summary: Valneva reported positive long-term antibody persistence data for its chikungunya vaccine IXCHIQ®, with 94% of participants maintaining neutralizing antibody levels five years after a single dose. The persistence was comparable across age groups (18-64 years and 65+ years), supporting the vaccine's differentiated profile for a disease with unpredictable epidemic outbreaks. The company continues to generate real-world evidence through post-commercialization studies, including a pilot vaccination campaign in Brazil that vaccinated approximately 80,000 adults.

RHHBY.summary: Roche announced new clinical data across its Alzheimer's disease portfolio at CTAD 2026, including Phase Ib/IIa data for trontinemab showing rapid amyloid removal, Phase III PrevenTRON study initiation for preclinical AD, and Phase II TARBELA-AD trial for NLRP3 inhibitor RG6434 targeting neuroinflammation. The company also highlighted its blood-based diagnostic tests Elecsys pTau217 and pTau181 for earlier and more accurate Alzheimer's diagnosis.

MERC.title: Mercer International Inc. Takes Next Step to Implement Recapitalization and Effectuate Balance Sheet Restructuring
MERC.summary: Mercer International Inc. has commenced a pre-packaged Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing with support from holders of over 88% of its senior notes. The restructuring aims to reduce senior note debt by approximately 88%, eliminate over $100 million in annual interest payments, and inject $400 million in new capital through a fully backstopped rights offering. The company expects to emerge by end of 2026 with operations continuing normally.

TLSA.summary: Tiziana Life Sciences announced positive topline results from its Phase 2a INFORM-MS trial of intranasal foralumab, a fully human anti-CD3 monoclonal antibody, for treating non-active secondary progressive multiple sclerosis (na-SPMS). CAPR.summary: Capricor Therapeutics announced that its HOPE-3 Phase 3 trial results for Deramiocel in Duchenne muscular dystrophy received the American Heart Association's Outstanding Research Award in Pediatric Cardiology.
